tooltip_popover.title: A Square and A Cube
tooltip_popover.content: Master topic for Chapter 1

tooltip_popover.title: 1.1 Perfect Squares and Square Roots
tooltip_popover.content: Theme section under A Square and A Cube

children.name: Definition and Geometric Representation of Perfect Squares

tooltip_popover.title: Definition and Geometric Representation of Perfect Squares
tooltip_popover.content: A perfect square is formed by multiplying a natural number by itself: n * n = n^2. The area of a square with side length x units is x^2 square units. Perfect squares always possess an odd count of total factors.
tooltip_popover.example: Queen Ratnamanjuri's Will Puzzle: Lockers remain open if and only if their locker numbers are perfect squares because they have an odd number of factors.

children.name: Ending Digits and Odd Sum Patterns of Squares

tooltip_popover.title: Ending Digits and Odd Sum Patterns of Squares
tooltip_popover.content: The unit digits of all perfect squares can only be 0, 1, 4, 5, 6, or 9. Numbers ending in 2, 3, 7, or 8 can never be perfect squares. The sum of the first n consecutive odd natural numbers starting from 1 is equal to n^2.

tooltip_popover.title: 1.2 Cubic Numbers and Cube Roots
tooltip_popover.content: Theme section under A Square and A Cube

children.name: Definition and Volume Scale of Perfect Cubes

tooltip_popover.title: Definition and Volume Scale of Perfect Cubes
tooltip_popover.content: A cubic number or perfect cube is obtained by multiplying a natural number by itself three times: n * n * n = n^3. A 3D cube of side 1 cm forms larger unit-cube assemblies of side 2 cm (8 cubes), side 3 cm (27 cubes), etc.
tooltip_popover.example: Unit Cubes Assembly: 3x3x3 block composed of 27 unit cubes.

children.name: Prime Factorisation Method for Square Roots and Cube Roots

tooltip_popover.title: Prime Factorisation Method for Square Roots and Cube Roots
tooltip_popover.content: Square roots require grouping prime factors into pairs of identical primes. Cube roots require grouping prime factors into triplets of identical primes. To convert a non-cube into a perfect cube, multiply or divide by missing factor powers.
tooltip_popover.example: Activity ACT-1.1: Finding cube root of 27000 via prime factorisation -> 27000 = (2*2*2)*(3*3*3)*(5*5*5) -> Cube Root = 2*3*5 = 30.

tooltip_popover.title: Power Play
tooltip_popover.content: Master topic for Chapter 2

tooltip_popover.title: 2.1 Multiplicative Growth and Exponents
tooltip_popover.content: Theme section under Power Play

tooltip_popover.title: Repeated Doubling and Exponential Notation
tooltip_popover.content: Multiplicative growth multiplies quantities repeatedly by a constant factor. In exponential expression a^n, 'a' represents the base and 'n' represents the exponent/power.
tooltip_popover.example: Magical Pond Lotus Problem: Lotuses double daily and cover pond on Day 30 -> Pond was half covered on Day 29.

children.name: 2.2 Laws of Exponents and Negative Powers

tooltip_popover.title: 2.2 Laws of Exponents and Negative Powers
tooltip_popover.content: Theme section under Power Play

tooltip_popover.title: Fundamental Laws of Exponents
tooltip_popover.content: Product Law: x^a * x^b = x^(a + b) Quotient Law: x^a / x^b = x^(a - b) Power of a Power Law: (x^a)^b = x^(a * b) Zero Exponent Law: x^0 = 1 for any non-zero x (derived from x^a / x^a = x^(a-a) = 1). Negative Exponent Law: x^(-n) = 1 / (x^n)

tooltip_popover.title: Scientific Notation and Practical Applications
tooltip_popover.content: Powers of 10 enable compact representation of vast and tiny quantities. Scientific notation represents numbers as m * 10^n where 1 <= m < 10.
tooltip_popover.example: Bacteria growth doubling every 20 mins: 100 bacteria after 2 hours (6 doubling periods) = 100 * 2^6 = 6400.

tooltip_popover.title: A Story of Numbers
tooltip_popover.content: Master topic for Chapter 3

tooltip_popover.title: 3.1 Counting and Landmark Numbers
tooltip_popover.content: Theme section under A Story of Numbers

children.name: Evolution of Counting and Landmark Symbols

tooltip_popover.title: Evolution of Counting and Landmark Symbols
tooltip_popover.content: Primitive counting relied on one-to-one matching with fingers, pebbles, and body parts. Civilizations developed landmark numbers to group large quantities without drawing repetitive tallies.
tooltip_popover.example: Roman Numeral System: Landmark symbols I (1), V (5), X (10), L (50), C (100), D (500), M (1000).

tooltip_popover.title: 3.2 Base-n and Place Value Systems
tooltip_popover.content: Theme section under A Story of Numbers

tooltip_popover.title: Comparison of Ancient Base Systems
tooltip_popover.content: Base-n systems select powers of n (n^0, n^1, n^2...) as uniform landmark values. Mesopotamian System: Base 60 (sexagesimal system), preserved today in 60-second minutes and 360-degree circles. Mayan System: Base 20 (vigesimal system). Hindu-Arabic System: Base 10 (decimal system) using positional place value.
tooltip_popover.example: Base-5 Construction Activity ACT-3.1: Grouping 5 ones into a 5-counter, 5 five-counters into a 25-counter. 23 in Base 10 = (43)_5.

children.name: The Hindu Decimal Place Value Revolution and Zero

tooltip_popover.title: The Hindu Decimal Place Value Revolution and Zero
tooltip_popover.content: The Hindu system introduced positional place value where a digit's position determines its magnitude. The symbol '0' served a dual purpose: a placeholder for empty positions and a standalone number. Eliminated the need for infinite new landmark symbols and streamlined arithmetic algorithms.
tooltip_popover.example: Efficiency comparison: In 375, '3' represents 3*10^2, whereas Roman numerals required cumbersome additive/subtractive notation (CCCLXXV).

tooltip_popover.title: Quadrilaterals
tooltip_popover.content: Master topic for Chapter 4

tooltip_popover.title: 4.1 Angle Sum Property and Rectangles
tooltip_popover.content: Theme section under Quadrilaterals

tooltip_popover.title: Interior Angle Sum of Quadrilaterals
tooltip_popover.content: Any closed 4-sided polygon (quadrilateral) divides into 2 interior triangles. Interior angle sum = 2 * 180 = 360 degrees: Angle A + Angle B + Angle C + Angle D = 360°.
tooltip_popover.example: If three interior angles of a quadrilateral are 90°, 80°, and 100°, the fourth angle equals 360° - 270° = 90°.

tooltip_popover.title: Properties of Rectangles
tooltip_popover.content: A rectangle is a quadrilateral with four equal 90° interior angles and opposite sides equal. Diagonals of a rectangle are equal in length and bisect each other.
tooltip_popover.example: Wooden Strip Rectangle Frame: Joining two equal wooden strips at their midpoints forms the diagonals of a rectangle regardless of intersection angle.

tooltip_popover.title: 4.2 Parallelograms, Rhombuses, and Squares
tooltip_popover.content: Theme section under Quadrilaterals

tooltip_popover.title: Parallelograms and Triangle Congruence Proofs
tooltip_popover.content: A parallelogram is a quadrilateral with both pairs of opposite sides parallel. Opposite sides are equal and opposite angles are equal. Adjacent angles are supplementary (add up to 180°).
tooltip_popover.example: Congruence Proof: Diagonal AC splits parallelogram ABCD into triangles ABC and CDA. ASA congruence proves opposite sides AB = CD and BC = DA.

tooltip_popover.title: Rhombuses, Squares, and Kites
tooltip_popover.content: Rhombus: Parallelogram with 4 equal sides; diagonals bisect each other at right angles (90°). Square: Combines all properties of a rectangle and a rhombus (4 equal sides, four 90° angles, equal perpendicular bisecting diagonals). Kite: Quadrilateral with two distinct pairs of equal adjacent sides and perpendicular diagonals.
tooltip_popover.example: Construction Activity ACT-4.1: Constructing a square with 6 cm diagonal using perpendicular bisectors.

tooltip_popover.title: Number Play
tooltip_popover.content: Master topic for Chapter 5

tooltip_popover.title: 5.1 Parity and Sums of Numbers
tooltip_popover.content: Theme section under Number Play

tooltip_popover.title: Parity Algebra and Operations
tooltip_popover.content: Parity defines whether an integer is even (2k) or odd (2k + 1). Addition Rules: Even + Even = Even, Odd + Odd = Even, Even + Odd = Odd. Multiplication Rules: Even * Even = Even, Odd * Odd = Odd, Even * Odd = Even.
tooltip_popover.example: Proof of sum of two odds: (2m + 1) + (2n + 1) = 2(m + n + 1), which is even.

tooltip_popover.title: 5.2 Generalised Form and Divisibility Proofs
tooltip_popover.content: Theme section under Number Play

tooltip_popover.title: Expanded Place Value Algebraic Notation
tooltip_popover.content: A 2-digit number 'ab' is expressed as 10a + b. A 3-digit number 'abc' is expressed as 100a + 10b + c. Reversing digits: (10a + b) - (10b + a) = 9(a - b), proving differences are always multiples of 9. 3-digit reversal difference: (100a + 10b + c) - (100c + 10b + a) = 99(a - c), always divisible by 99.
tooltip_popover.example: Reversing Digits Puzzle ACT-5.1: Proving algebraic divisibility by 9.

tooltip_popover.title: Proofs for Standard Divisibility Rules
tooltip_popover.content: Divisibility by 2: 10a + b = 2(5a) + b -> depends solely on unit digit b being even. Divisibility by 4: 100a + (10b + c) = 4(25a) + (10b + c) -> depends on last two digits (10b + c). Divisibility by 3/9: 100a + 10b + c = 99a + 9b + (a + b + c) -> depends on digit sum (a + b + c). Divisibility by 11: Alternating sum difference of odd-place and even-place digits is 0 or multiple of 11.
tooltip_popover.example: 214365 digit sum = 21 (not divisible by 9, so number is not divisible by 9).

tooltip_popover.title: We Distribute, Yet Things Multiply
tooltip_popover.content: Master topic for Chapter 6

tooltip_popover.title: 6.1 Distributive Property and Expansion
tooltip_popover.content: Theme section under We Distribute, Yet Things Multiply

tooltip_popover.title: Algebraic Expansion via Distributive Law
tooltip_popover.content: Single term distribution: a(b + c) = ab + ac. Binomial distribution: (a + b)(c + d) = a(c + d) + b(c + d) = ac + ad + bc + bd. Like terms contain identical variables raised to identical powers and can be combined.
tooltip_popover.example: Geometric Area Model: A rectangle with sides (a+b) and (c+d) partitions into 4 sub-rectangles with areas ac, ad, bc, and bd.

tooltip_popover.title: 6.2 Standard Algebraic Identities
tooltip_popover.content: Theme section under We Distribute, Yet Things Multiply

tooltip_popover.title: Core Algebraic Identities
tooltip_popover.content: Identity 1 (Square of Sum): (a + b)^2 = a^2 + 2ab + b^2 Identity 2 (Square of Difference): (a - b)^2 = a^2 - 2ab + b^2 Identity 3 (Difference of Squares): (a + b)(a - b) = a^2 - b^2 Trinomial Square: (a + b + c)^2 = a^2 + b^2 + c^2 + 2ab + 2bc + 2ca.
tooltip_popover.example: Paper Cutout Activity ACT-6.1: Visual verification of (a+b)^2 by assembling a^2, b^2, and two ab rectangles.

tooltip_popover.title: Proportional Reasoning-1
tooltip_popover.content: Master topic for Chapter 7

tooltip_popover.title: 7.1 Ratios and Scaling Factors
tooltip_popover.content: Theme section under Proportional Reasoning-1

children.name: Concept of Ratio and Equivalent Multipliers

tooltip_popover.title: Concept of Ratio and Equivalent Multipliers
tooltip_popover.content: A ratio compares two quantities of the same unit through division: a:b = a/b. Simplifying ratios requires dividing both antecedent and consequent by their Highest Common Factor (HCF). Proportional scaling requires multiplying or dividing all terms by a constant factor k.
tooltip_popover.example: Lemonade Recipe Scaling: Doubling lemon juice and water preserves taste because ratio 1:5 stays constant.

tooltip_popover.title: 7.2 Solving Proportions and Unit Rates
tooltip_popover.content: Theme section under Proportional Reasoning-1

children.name: Proportion Laws and Unit Rate Applications

tooltip_popover.title: Proportion Laws and Unit Rate Applications
tooltip_popover.content: A proportion equates two ratios: a/b = c/d. Cross Product Property: Product of extremes equals product of means (a * d = b * c). Unit Rate Method: Calculates the value for 1 unit first before scaling to the required quantity.
tooltip_popover.example: Checking proportion: 4, 8, 12, 24 -> 4*24 = 96 and 8*12 = 96 -> forms a valid proportion.
